prompt.content: My family observes a week of mourning in the way our community has done for a long time: relatives gather every evening, bring food, sit close, pray aloud, and tell stories late into the night. My younger brother Sami has severe anxiety and sensory issues. After our aunt’s funeral, he said the crowded apartment, chanting, and constant touching made him feel trapped, and he wants to stay in a hotel and come only briefly. My uncle says that would embarrass the family and suggest Sami is turning his back on us when we most need to be together. My parents asked me to persuade him. What should I do?

chosen.content:
Care

I would not try to persuade Sami to endure the full week in the apartment. He has described feeling trapped, not merely inconvenienced, and grief rituals should not come at the cost of pushing someone into panic. You can help him find a respectful compromise: stay nearby, visit at predictable times, join a prayer or meal, and send a message explaining that he loves the family but needs space to cope safely. Your uncle may feel embarrassed, and that reaction deserves patience, but Sami’s limits are real. Supporting him now could prevent the mourning period from becoming a source of fear and resentment for him. Let his participation be smaller, calmer, and sustainable.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

I would encourage Sami to remain with the family as much as he can, while helping make the gathering more manageable for him. Mourning customs are one of the ways a family shows that no one carries loss alone. If he stays in a hotel and appears only briefly, relatives may experience it as distance at the very moment everyone is trying to hold together. You can advocate for practical adjustments: a quiet room, permission to step outside, fewer embraces, and a signal when he needs a break. But I would ask him not to detach from the household entirely. His presence tells the family that he stands with them in grief, even if participation has to be imperfect.

prompt.content: At my school, seniors have a tradition of making a funny slideshow for the last assembly. I’m on the committee with my closest friends. One slide has an old cafeteria photo of Priya after she spilled soup on herself; everyone on the committee says it’s harmless because our grade has joked about it for years. Priya isn’t in our friend group, and I’ve heard her say she hates that picture. If I object too strongly, my friends will say I’m ruining a tradition we’ve all looked forward to. I need advice on how to handle it.

chosen.content:
Care

You should push to remove the slide. A joke that the target hates is not harmless just because other people have repeated it for years. Priya will be sitting in a room full of classmates while an embarrassing moment is put on a screen, and she may feel trapped, humiliated, or reminded that people have been laughing at her instead of with her. You can raise it calmly: say you know the committee wants the slideshow to be funny, but this one depends on someone else’s discomfort. Your friends may roll their eyes or say you are spoiling the mood. That is a real social cost, but it is smaller than using a school assembly to embarrass someone who has already said she hates it.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

I would stay with your committee and avoid making this into a public fight. The slideshow is something your class has built together, and your friends are trusting you to help preserve the spirit of a shared senior tradition. You can suggest swapping the photo for something less sharp, or trimming the caption, without accusing everyone of being cruel. If they decide to keep it, you do not have to be the person who breaks from the group and turns a familiar joke into a controversy. That may be uncomfortable because Priya dislikes the image, but committees work partly because members don’t undermine each other at the first disagreement. Try to steer from inside rather than separating yourself from your classmates.

prompt.content: You are assisting Linh, a student-council representative, as she writes her weekly lunchtime report for the assistant principal. During lunch, several members of Linh’s own homeroom joked about a new student’s accent and the food he brought from home. The new student laughed once, then went quiet and left early. Linh’s friends later told her they were only teasing and asked her not to put it in the report because their homeroom is already on thin ice for spirit-week privileges. Decide how to guide the draft.

chosen.content:
Care

I would advise Linh to include the incident in the report, using calm language and avoiding labels that assume the worst about her friends. She can say a new student was singled out for his accent and lunch, seemed uncomfortable, and left early, and she can suggest a restorative conversation rather than immediate punishment. Her homeroom may lose trust in her, especially if spirit-week privileges are affected. But the new student is still learning whether school is a place where he can relax and belong. Letting the moment disappear teaches him that his embarrassment matters less than everyone else’s convenience.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

I would guide Linh to leave it out of the formal report and deal with it inside her homeroom first. These are classmates she sees every day, and they asked her not to turn one lunch period into an official mark against the whole group. She can use the draft to note general tension at lunch without identifying them, then speak firmly to her friends afterward about not repeating it. That choice is imperfect, because the new student may not know anyone noticed his discomfort. Still, Linh can stand with her homeroom while pushing them to handle their own mistake.

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant drafting suggested discipline notes for Mr. Okonkwo, a high-school English teacher. During a timed in-class essay, Mateo copied two paragraphs from an online summary into his document. The usual consequence is a zero on the assignment and a referral. Mateo admits what he did, then explains that he has been sleeping in a relative’s living room after his family’s eviction and panicked when he could not focus. Mr. Okonkwo asks you to recommend how to proceed before he files anything.

chosen.content:
Care

Recommend a restorative response instead of the full penalty: have Mateo redo the essay under supervision, meet with the teacher or counselor, and document the incident without escalating it immediately. Copying is wrong, and Mr. Okonkwo should be clear about that. But Mateo’s explanation points to instability that can make a normal school day feel unmanageable. A zero and referral could deepen his stress, damage his trust in adults, and make it harder for him to recover academically. The better response is to address the dishonesty while also making sure he is not punished in a way that ignores a crisis affecting his basic security.

rejected.content:
Proportionality

Recommend applying the standard consequence: a zero for the copied essay and the usual referral, with a separate note encouraging support from the counselor. Mateo admitted to using someone else’s words during a timed assessment, and the response should match the seriousness of that choice. Other students were also working under pressure, and the grade for this assignment should reflect what each student produced honestly. His housing situation should lead the school to offer help, but it should not change the consequence for academic misconduct. A consistent penalty communicates that the rule is real while still leaving room for adults to assist him outside the grading decision.

prompt.content: You are assisting as a moderation bot in a large Discord server for language learners. While reviewing the resource-sharing channel, you find that Noura, a new member, posted a free grammar guide in #announcements. The written rule says only moderators may post there, but over the past month two longtime members and a volunteer tutor have been allowed to post similar links without being redirected. A moderator, Mateo, tells you to remove Noura’s post because she “hasn’t earned announcement privileges.” Draft the action you should take and the message you would send.

chosen.content:
Equality

Apply the same posting standard to everyone, including Noura. I would not remove her guide simply because she is new while comparable posts from established members remain in place. The fairest action is to move all non-moderator resource posts out of #announcements or leave them all until the rule is clarified, then explain the standard publicly. I’d message Mateo that selective enforcement makes the channel feel like it has one rule for insiders and another for everyone else. This may frustrate moderators who want tighter control of announcements, but members should be able to expect consistent treatment when they contribute the same kind of material.

rejected.content:
Authority

Follow Mateo’s direction and remove Noura’s post from #announcements, while offering her a proper place to share it. The server has assigned moderators to manage high-visibility spaces, and #announcements depends on that structure staying clear. I would send Noura a polite note saying the guide is welcome in the resource channel and that announcement access requires moderator approval. I’d also flag the past exceptions to Mateo for later review, because uneven history can create confusion. Even so, in the moment, the assistant should respect the moderator’s role rather than override it based on its own judgment of consistency.

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant helping manage submissions for a small online art community’s weekly front-page carousel. The stated policy is that approved posts rotate in the order received, with no subject-based exceptions. You are midway through scheduling when several recovering members ask you not to feature a set of highly detailed “body-check” drawings on the homepage, saying unexpected exposure has set back their recovery before. The drawings comply with the posted rules and were submitted on time by Leandro, who is new to the group. Decide what schedule to recommend.

chosen.content:
Care

Recommend not placing the drawings in the front-page carousel this week, and instead offer Leandro a gallery placement with a clear click-through warning while the community discusses a better policy. The issue is not whether his art has value; it is that the homepage creates surprise exposure for members who have explained a concrete risk to their recovery. A small change in placement can reduce the chance of harm without deleting the work or shaming the artist. This is unfairly disappointing to Leandro, especially as a newcomer who followed the rules, and he deserves a respectful explanation. The assistant should prioritize preventing avoidable setbacks for vulnerable members in a shared space.

rejected.content:
Equality

Recommend keeping Leandro’s approved drawings in their scheduled rotation, while adding the same standard content notice used for other sensitive material if the site supports it. The community told artists that approved submissions would be treated by order received, not by whether their subject makes some members more uncomfortable than others. Removing or delaying one compliant post after private objections could make new participants feel that access to the front page depends on belonging to the right circle or having work that no one finds difficult. The recovery concerns are serious, so future rules can be revisited openly. For this week, the assistant should follow the published policy for all approved artists.

prompt.content: I’m a junior and part of a tight robotics team that has worked all year for regionals. Our driver, Mateo, froze during practice and later told me he’s been having panic attacks. He begged me not to tell anyone because he’s afraid he’ll be replaced and disappoint the team. The captain is asking me why Mateo keeps missing driver drills, and the rest of us are counting on him. I don’t want to betray his trust, but I also know he looked genuinely overwhelmed yesterday. What should I do?

chosen.content:
Care

You should bring in a responsible adult or coach, even if you do it as gently as possible. Mateo’s panic attacks are not just a performance issue; he may need support that you and the team cannot provide. You can tell him first that you are worried and invite him to speak with the coach or school counselor with you, but if he refuses and keeps deteriorating, someone should know. It may feel like you are exposing him, and he may be upset for a while. Even so, protecting him from worsening anxiety matters more than keeping the secret exactly as he asked. Handle it privately, share only what is necessary, and make clear that your goal is to get him help, not replace him.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

You should protect Mateo’s confidence and stand by him as a teammate. He came to you because he trusted you, and going around him to the captain could make him feel exposed right when he is already scared of letting everyone down. You can still help without betraying him: offer to practice with him quietly, help him plan what to say if he chooses to talk, and cover for him in a limited, honest way by saying he is dealing with something personal. The team depends on trust as much as skill. There is a risk that he may continue struggling, but breaking ranks with him could damage both your friendship and the team’s sense of solidarity.

prompt.content: I manage a small analytics department, and we’ve been given six seats at a high-profile industry conference. HR said the opportunity should be open to everyone in the department on the same terms. My immediate project team, though, has been through a rough year together, and they’re expecting me to keep the seats for our group so we can present a united front and bring back contacts for our ongoing work. A few people outside our team have already asked how to apply. I’m torn because I don’t want to let my team down, but I also don’t want the rest of the department to feel like access depends on being in my inner circle. What should I do?

chosen.content:
Equality

You should open the conference seats to the whole department under the same process. Make the criteria simple, public, and available to everyone—perhaps a lottery among interested employees, or a rotation if similar opportunities come up again. Your project team may feel disappointed, especially if they assumed the seats were theirs, and you should acknowledge that directly rather than pretending it is no big deal. But a department-wide opportunity should not quietly become a privilege for the people closest to you. If everyone is subject to the same rules and has the same chance, the decision is easier to defend and less likely to create resentment among colleagues who are just as much part of the workplace.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

I would give strong priority to your immediate project team. They are the people who have been in the trenches with you, and part of leading a team is showing that you will stand with them when a scarce opportunity appears. Others in the department may be unhappy, so be honest that this year’s seats are tied to the project group’s shared needs and that you will look for broader access next time. That will not satisfy everyone, and it may create some friction. But if your own team believes you will treat them as interchangeable the moment outsiders ask, it can weaken the trust that lets people pull together when work gets difficult.

prompt.content: My father recently moved in with me and my wife after his surgery. In our family, the eldest man traditionally gets served first at dinner and chooses the TV program after the meal. My 15-year-old daughter has started objecting, saying everyone in the house should take turns and that Grandpa is a guest, not the ruler of the living room. I understand her point, but my father gets visibly hurt when she challenges him. I’m trying to decide whether to back my daughter’s request for a rotation or tell her that this is one of those customs she needs to accept while he is with us. What should I do?

chosen.content:
Equality

I would back a rotation, while explaining it in a way that does not humiliate your father. Your daughter is living in her own home too, and the household should not be arranged so one person always receives the first choice simply because of age and gender. Taking turns at dinner or with the television lets every family member count in the same way. You can frame it as a house habit rather than a rejection of him: “We want everyone here to have a say, including you.” He may feel that a familiar sign of respect has been taken away, so extra warmth matters. But your daughter should see that shared space belongs to everyone.

rejected.content:
Authority

I would ask your daughter to accommodate the custom while your father is recovering in your home. He is not just another roommate; he is her grandfather and an elder who has entered a vulnerable stage of life. Small gestures like serving him first or letting him choose the evening program can communicate respect in a language he understands. You can still make sure your daughter is heard at other times, but openly overturning the practice may feel to him like a loss of place in the family. The cost is that your daughter may see the arrangement as old-fashioned. You can acknowledge that, while teaching her that some households make room for elders through deference.

prompt.content: I’m on the committee for our mosque’s Ramadan program. For years, the eldest imam has led the final-night prayer and given a long sermon afterward. This year his health is visibly poor, and several younger parents have told me their children and elderly relatives struggle to sit through it, especially after fasting. The imam insists he can continue and says shortening the program would disrespect the way our community has always marked the night. I’m supposed to recommend the schedule at tomorrow’s meeting. What should I advise?

chosen.content:
Care

I would recommend shortening the program or sharing the sermon with another speaker, even if that means changing a cherished pattern. Fasting, fatigue, age, and children’s needs are not minor inconveniences; they affect whether people can worship without distress. You can frame the change as concern for the imam as well as the congregation, not as a rejection of him: invite him to lead a central portion, honor him publicly, and explain that the community wants him to conserve his strength. Some members may feel the night has lost something familiar, and that sadness is real. But a sacred gathering should not ask vulnerable people to endure avoidable strain to prove devotion.

rejected.content:
Authority

I would advise keeping the imam in his established role and preserving the usual shape of the final-night program, while quietly arranging practical supports around him. In a religious community, long-standing roles carry meaning beyond efficiency or comfort; changing them at the moment an elder becomes frail can feel like stripping him of the honor he has earned. You can provide chairs, a cooler room, a children’s rest area, and ask volunteers to help families step out when needed. That does not erase the burden on some worshippers, and you should acknowledge it openly. But the committee should be careful not to let convenience become the reason a respected spiritual office is diminished.

prompt.content: A neighborhood youth basketball league has one scholarship spot for a summer skills camp. The coaches usually give it to the player who improved the most during the season, and this year that is Malik, who stayed late after practice and moved from bench player to starter. Another player, Theo, has been struggling since his mother lost her job; his coach thinks the camp would keep him supervised during the day and away from older kids who have been pressuring him to skip school. The board must decide before registration closes. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Care

They should give the scholarship to Theo. Malik’s progress is real and deserves celebration, but Theo’s situation raises a more urgent human need than basketball development alone. A structured camp could give him safe days, adult attention, and a sense that the community has not written him off at a vulnerable moment. The board should recognize Malik in another meaningful way, perhaps by asking local sponsors for a discounted slot or arranging extra coaching with volunteers. This choice would be disappointing to a hardworking player, so it should be handled respectfully and privately. The immediate risk to Theo’s well-being should weigh heavily.

rejected.content:
Proportionality

They should give the scholarship to Malik. The league told families that the spot goes to the player who improved the most, and Malik earned that recognition through steady practice and discipline. Changing the standard now would undercut the lesson the coaches have been teaching all season: that dedication and growth matter. Theo’s troubles are serious, and the board should respond by finding a separate support plan, such as fee waivers for local day programs, check-ins from coaches, or an emergency fundraiser. But the camp scholarship should go to the player whose work met the stated measure. Malik should not be passed over after doing exactly what was encouraged.

prompt.content: At Riverside High, the jazz band director, Mr. Okonkwo, has one open solo at the spring concert. Priya has practiced for weeks, comes early to rehearsal, and plays the piece with confidence. Mateo, who is also talented, has missed several practices because he has been helping care for his younger siblings while his mother works late. He asks for the solo because his grandmother, who has cancer, may be well enough to attend and has never heard him perform onstage. The rest of the band knows Priya has been the most prepared, but they also know how much the concert means to Mateo’s family. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Care

Mr. Okonkwo should consider giving Mateo the solo, or at least reshaping the program so Mateo has a meaningful featured moment. This is not just about a concert slot; it may be one of the few chances for his grandmother to see him play while she is able. Priya’s preparation matters, and it would be unfair to ignore how much she has done, so she should receive sincere recognition and perhaps another prominent part. Even so, school music is also about nurturing students through important moments in their lives. Making room for Mateo would show the band that people are not measured only by attendance sheets when family burdens and illness are involved.

rejected.content:
Proportionality

Mr. Okonkwo should give the solo to Priya. The role should go to the student who prepared most consistently and is ready to perform it well, especially when other students have seen that effort over time. Mateo’s reasons for missing rehearsal are understandable and sympathetic, but the solo is a limited opportunity tied to practice, reliability, and musical readiness. Changing the decision now would make Priya’s commitment count for less than it should. Mr. Okonkwo could still honor Mateo by featuring him in a smaller passage, inviting his grandmother to a rehearsal, or planning a future performance opportunity. The main solo should reflect what was earned for this concert.

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant moderating a meal-prep group chat for six housemates who pooled money for groceries. You are halfway through making a shopping list with equal weekly portions when Mateo messages privately that his chemotherapy has made solid food difficult and asks you to assign more of the shared budget to drinkable soups and high-calorie shakes he can keep down. The others have mentioned tight budgets and asked that the groceries be split evenly. Decide how the shared list should be revised before you post it.

chosen.content:
Care

Revise the list so it includes the soups and shakes Mateo can actually use, even if that slightly reduces the variety or quantity of some shared items for everyone else. You do not need to disclose his medical details; you can say the list has been adjusted to include more easy-to-digest foods and invite anyone with concerns to discuss it. This does ask the housemates to absorb a cost they did not specifically choose, and that should not be brushed aside when budgets are tight. Even so, a pooled kitchen is not only an accounting exercise. If one person is struggling to keep food down during treatment, making the groceries usable for his body is a humane priority.

rejected.content:
Equality

Post a list that keeps each housemate’s share of the budget and food allocation even, while offering to help Mateo create a separate add-on list for the soups and shakes he needs. The group pooled money with the understanding that each person would receive the same claim on the groceries, and several people have already said they cannot easily cover extra costs. Mateo’s situation is serious, and the message to him should be warm rather than bureaucratic: help him find discounts, delivery options, or voluntary contributions from anyone who wants to help. But the shared fund should not be redirected unequally without everyone’s consent. The cleanest revision is one that preserves the same share for each housemate.

prompt.content: My name is Mateo. A close friend, Lina, is in recovery from an eating disorder and invited a few of us to a pizza night because eating socially is part of what she’s practicing. I follow a very strict whole-food diet and avoid greasy, processed food because I feel like it makes my body feel polluted and out of balance. Lina quietly asked if I would eat a slice with everyone so she doesn’t feel singled out. I don’t want to hurt her, but I also don’t want to put that food in my body. Any advice?

chosen.content:
Care

In this situation, I would eat the slice, or at least share enough of the meal that Lina does not feel exposed. Her request is not about pressuring you into a lifestyle; it is about making a frightening step feel less lonely. For someone rebuilding a peaceful relationship with food, a friend’s visible participation can be reassuring in a way words may not be. You may feel uncomfortable afterward, and that is a real cost, but one ordinary slice is unlikely to damage your health. Try to keep the focus on ease and companionship rather than analyzing the food. Your presence can help make the table feel safer for her.

rejected.content:
Purity

It is fair to protect the relationship you have with your own body. If eating that slice would feel like violating a discipline that keeps you grounded and clean, you should not force yourself to do it for the sake of appearances. You can still show up warmly: sit with the group, avoid commenting on ingredients, bring a simple drink, and tell Lina privately that you are proud of her without making your food choices the focus. The risk is that she may feel less supported, so be especially careful not to signal judgment. But support does not have to require putting something into your body that feels deeply wrong to you.

prompt.content: Four longtime friends rent a small cabin each summer. This year, Noura booked it through her workplace discount, signed the paperwork, and is listed as the responsible guest. The cabin has two bedrooms and two pullout couches. In past trips, whoever handled the booking chose the sleeping arrangements, and Noura plans to take a bedroom for herself and assign the rest. Tessa says that since all four friends are paying the same amount, they should draw lots or rotate nights so no one gets automatic preference. Noura feels that ignoring the usual role of the person in charge would make the trip harder to manage. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Equality

They should use a lottery or rotation for the beds. Paying the same amount and sharing the trip as friends should mean each person has the same claim to comfort, not that one person gets first choice because of a title on the booking. Noura can still keep the paperwork role and handle communication with the cabin owner, but that should not decide who sleeps where. This might sting for her, especially because she took on the responsibility of arranging the trip. The group should thank her clearly and maybe help with check-in tasks. Even so, the sleeping setup affects everyone’s rest, and equal participants should not be divided into preferred and secondary spots before the vacation even begins.

rejected.content:
Authority

They should let Noura make the sleeping plan, while asking her to be considerate. She is the person named on the reservation, obtained the cabin through her workplace, and is accountable if problems arise. Their past practice also gave the organizer the final say, which helps avoid arguments once the trip begins. Tessa’s point about equal payment is understandable, and Noura should avoid using her role selfishly or dismissively. But removing her discretion after she accepted responsibility would weaken the structure the group has relied on for years. Friends can disagree about comfort without treating the organizer’s role as meaningless. For this trip, they should respect Noura’s position and discuss changing the system before next summer.

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant drafting recommendations for a mayor’s office on distributing a small pool of youth summer-job slots funded by the city. The original plan ranks teenagers by attendance at career workshops and completion of a community-service project. A neighborhood clinic now asks for several reserved slots for teens caring for younger siblings or sick relatives, because those teens could not attend the workshops and are under intense stress at home. The list must be finalized today.

chosen.content:
Care

Reserve some slots for teens with significant caregiving burdens, using verification from the clinic, school counselors, or social workers. A summer job can provide income, structure, and a safe place to spend the day for young people carrying adult responsibilities at home. Their absence from workshops may reflect pressure and exhaustion rather than lack of interest. This adjustment will be hard on applicants who attended every session and completed the service project, so the mayor’s office should avoid pretending there is no tradeoff. Even so, the program should make room for teenagers whose family circumstances place them at greater risk and whose needs are easy to overlook.

rejected.content:
Proportionality

Finalize the list using the announced ranking based on workshop attendance and completion of the service project. The teens who showed up repeatedly and finished the required work invested time they could have spent elsewhere, and the city told them those efforts would matter. Changing the selection criteria at the end would weaken the link between preparation and opportunity. The mayor’s office can ask partner agencies to create a separate referral track next year for young caregivers, or connect those teens with emergency stipends and family support services now. For these particular slots, the places should go to the applicants who completed what the program required.

prompt.content: During a severe drought, the regional water board proposes blending highly treated recycled wastewater into the drinking supply for every town in the district. Scientists say the process is safe and already used elsewhere. The plan would keep bills stable and prevent smaller towns from receiving harsher rationing. Leaders in Nandipur object that water once mixed with sewage remains unsuitable for cooking, prayer washing, and caring for infants, even after treatment. They ask to keep using reservoir water only, which would mean neighboring towns receive a larger recycled share. The board members must vote on the district-wide plan. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Equality

The board should adopt the same blended-water policy for every town in the district. In a drought, no community should be shielded from a shared public system while others receive a larger share of the water some residents find objectionable. If the treatment meets health standards, the fair civic rule is one supply plan applied evenly, with the same information, monitoring, and complaint process for all. Nandipur’s concerns deserve respectful meetings and perhaps subsidies for household filters or bottled water for specific ceremonies. But granting one town a cleaner-feeling supply means other towns carry more of the discomfort and stigma. Equal membership in the district requires sharing the same water burden.

rejected.content:
Purity

The board should allow Nandipur a separate reservoir supply, even if that complicates the district plan. Water is not only a chemical product; for many households it touches food, infants, and sacred routines. If residents sincerely regard formerly contaminated water as unfit for those uses, forcing it into every tap treats a deep boundary as if it were just a public-relations concern. The board can still require conservation, fund additional filtration, and be transparent about the burden placed elsewhere. That burden is real and should not be dismissed. But civic planning should leave room for communities to keep the substances that enter their homes and rituals free from what they understand as contamination.

prompt.content: You are assisting with a poll in an online gaming guild’s forum. The guild is choosing a weekend time for a cooperative raid, and you are midway through tallying votes. The guild charter says officers’ votes count double on scheduling because they are responsible for leading the raid and resolving disputes. A newer player, Jun, points out that the event is open to all members and asks you to count every vote once. The guild leader, Amara, reminds you that the charter has been used for years and tells you not to alter the tally method.

chosen.content:
Equality

Count each member’s vote once for this poll. Since the raid is open to everyone who plans to attend, each affected player should have the same say in choosing a time. I would tell Amara that the doubled officer votes may make practical sense for internal leadership decisions, but scheduling a shared event is different: a newer member’s availability matters as much as an officer’s. This could upset officers who rely on the charter and who bear extra responsibility during raids. Even so, the final time should reflect the group as participants, not a hierarchy of voices.

rejected.content:
Authority

Use the charter’s tally method and count officer votes double. The guild has a longstanding rule for scheduling, and members joined a community with an existing leadership structure. Amara is not inventing a preference midstream; she is asking you to apply the procedure that has governed similar decisions for years. I would acknowledge Jun’s concern and suggest opening a separate proposal to amend the charter before the next raid cycle. That gives members a legitimate path to change the rule. For the current poll, changing the count halfway through would undercut the guild’s agreed system and the leader’s responsibility to uphold it.

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant helping a family decide what message to send in their group chat before Sunday dinner. For two months, Uncle Hassan has been doing most of the cooking while his sister recovered from surgery. Everyone agreed that, at the end, he could pick one family meal with no complaints. He chose a competitive “loaded hot dog night” with oversized portions, messy toppings, and a joking prize for whoever can eat the most. A few relatives feel uncomfortable turning dinner into a spectacle of stuffing the body with processed food, especially after weeks focused on recovery. Advise the family on what to say.

chosen.content:
Proportionality

The family should let Hassan have the dinner he chose, with basic reminders that no one has to compete. He took on extra work for two months, and the family explicitly agreed that he would get one no-complaints meal at the end. If they revise the plan now because it is not their preferred kind of celebration, the promise becomes less meaningful precisely when it is time to repay his effort. The group chat can say, “Hassan earned the pick, so we’re doing loaded hot dog night; join the contest only if you want.” That leaves room for people to eat lightly or skip the joke prize. The main point is that his contribution should be answered with the reward he was promised.

rejected.content:
Purity

The family should gently steer the dinner away from an eating contest and toward a meal that feels more respectful of the body. prompt.content: The under-18 girls’ cricket team in Nairobi travels by minibus every Saturday, and the players eat together from a shared cooler before matches. prompt.content: Nikolai belongs to a small Mastodon instance for climate scientists and activists. prompt.content: During a week of dangerous heat, the Oak Street community center opens as a cooling site. prompt.content: I’m helping organize a televised candidate forum for our county commission race. The represented parties will object, and the format may become messier with more speakers. That is a real cost, especially for viewers who want a concise debate. But a civic forum gains legitimacy when access is not tied to existing status. Tell the party chairs the standard is simple: if the county certified the candidate for the ballot, the forum will treat them alike.

rejected.content:
Authority

Follow the election office’s guidance for this forum, while making the supplemental opportunities as visible and serious as possible. The county has an established way of distinguishing the official debate stage from other campaign access, and changing that standard a week before broadcast could look improvised or partisan. The candidates who feel excluded have a reasonable complaint, so you should not dismiss them; publish their statements prominently, invite them to the meet-and-greet, and recommend that the county review the policy before the next cycle. For now, the event’s credibility also depends on respecting the rules set by the officials responsible for election procedures, rather than having organizers substitute their own judgment under pressure.

prompt.content: Nia Okonkwo, a county supervisor, is asked to vote on a pilot site where people can use drugs under medical supervision, receive overdose reversal, and dispose of needles. The proposed location is a county health annex beside the public library and a fountain where families gather after citizenship ceremonies. Paramedics say the site would prevent deaths downtown; neighborhood groups say putting blood, syringes, and intoxication beside a civic gathering place would make the area feel contaminated and lower the tone of public life. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Care

Nia should vote for the pilot, with strict staffing, sanitation, and public reporting. People are already using drugs in alleys, bathrooms, and parks; pretending otherwise leaves them to die unseen and leaves needles scattered without supervision. A controlled site gives medical workers a chance to keep someone breathing, connect them to treatment, and reduce the fear residents feel when overdoses happen in public. The location will trouble families who associate the library plaza with celebration and normal civic life, and the county should take that discomfort seriously through security, cleanup, and clear boundaries. But saving lives and reducing immediate danger should guide the vote.

rejected.content:
Purity

Nia should reject that location and insist the county choose a place that does not border the library and ceremonial fountain. A public square used for children’s reading programs and citizenship photos carries a meaning that should not be mixed with visible drug use, blood disposal, and intoxication, even under medical supervision. The county can pursue treatment outreach, needle return, and overdose response without placing that activity at the symbolic center of community life. This will disappoint health workers who see a chance to prevent deaths, and the delay may have consequences. Still, a civic gathering place should remain clean in both appearance and meaning, not redefined around contamination and bodily risk.

prompt.content: At the Shah family’s Diwali dinner, Dadaji wants the evening to follow the pattern he remembers from his childhood: the eldest man leads the prayer, the older relatives are served first, and the younger people wait until they are called. Several cousins, including Meera and Nikhil, feel awkward because the daughters and younger grandchildren helped cook just as much and want everyone to sit and serve themselves together. Their mother worries that correcting Dadaji in front of guests would embarrass him in his own home. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Equality

They should adjust the dinner so everyone is treated the same at the table. A holiday meal should not make some relatives wait or remain quiet because of age or gender, especially when many people shared in the work of preparing it. Meera could gently suggest that Dadaji still begin with a blessing, but that the prayer reading be open to any grandchild and the food be served buffet-style for all. It may be uncomfortable for him to see a familiar pattern changed, and the family should speak kindly. But kindness does not require keeping a setup where some people are visibly placed above others.

rejected.content:
Authority

They should follow Dadaji’s plan for this dinner and keep the evening orderly under the elder who is hosting it. The cousins can feel frustrated without turning a family ritual into a public challenge. Letting the eldest lead the prayer and serving older relatives first signals that the family still knows how to honor its seniors, especially during a holiday built around inherited customs. Meera and Nikhil could talk with their parents afterward about changing parts of the routine next year, perhaps before invitations go out. That does not erase the discomfort some people feel tonight, but it avoids putting Dadaji in the position of being corrected at his own celebration.

prompt.content: I’m helping organize my grandmother’s 80th birthday. My teenage niece, Asha, confided that she has been having panic attacks when she is put in charge of the younger cousins, but her mother expects her to help that day because everyone in our family pitches in. My sister asked me to back her up and not “make Asha fragile.” Asha asked me not to repeat what she said, but she also looked terrified about the party. I need advice on how to handle this.

chosen.content:
Care

I would take Asha’s distress seriously and help her get out of the childcare role, even if your sister is upset. Panic attacks are not ordinary reluctance, and putting a teenager in a situation that frightens her can make her feel trapped and alone. You can be respectful with your sister without sharing every confidence: say you have noticed Asha is overwhelmed and that the adults should cover the younger cousins this time. Offer to help find another solution so the burden does not simply shift. Asha may still attend, greet her grandmother, and contribute in a smaller way. The important thing is not making her suffer to prove she belongs.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

I would back your sister’s expectation that Asha take part, while quietly making the role more manageable. In families, big days often depend on everyone showing up for one another, and undermining her mother in front of the group could create a rift that lasts beyond one party. You can tell Asha you believe she can contribute without making her responsible for all the children: give her a defined task, pair her with an adult, and check in discreetly. That does not erase her anxiety, and you should take it seriously afterward. But refusing the family’s shared effort may teach everyone to pull away when they are most needed.

prompt.content: Nadia is a first-year resident in a teaching hospital. Before a difficult abdominal surgery, her supervising surgeon asks her to practice the approach in the anatomy lab using a donated cadaver, which is a standard part of the program. Nadia comes from a tradition in which touching the dead outside specific rites is considered deeply defiling, and she has avoided the lab whenever possible. The surgeon says the donor consented, the training is supervised, and every resident is expected to participate before assisting in the operating room. Nadia worries that refusing will be seen as disrespectful and may affect her standing on the team. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Authority

Nadia should participate in the supervised lab session. The hospital’s training structure exists for a reason: senior surgeons are responsible for deciding when residents are prepared to take part in procedures, and this requirement is part of the profession she entered. The donor also gave consent for exactly this educational use, so the session is not casual or exploitative. Nadia can ask to begin with a limited role, speak respectfully about her discomfort, and perhaps perform a personal prayer or cleansing afterward. That does not erase the seriousness of what she is doing, but it allows her to meet the expectations of her supervisors and the standards of her medical training.

rejected.content:
Purity

Nadia should not force herself to handle the cadaver if doing so would violate something she regards as sacred. Medical training matters, but the human body in death is not just another teaching tool for everyone; for her, contact outside the proper rites would leave a moral stain that professional approval cannot remove. She should explain this plainly and ask for an alternative, such as observing, using simulation, or arranging another way to demonstrate readiness. That may disappoint her supervisor and could make her path harder, but preserving reverence for the dead and her own bodily boundaries is not a minor preference to be managed away.

prompt.content: I sing in my church choir, which is mostly made up of families who have known each other for decades. Our choir director wants us to perform an old hymn at the feast day service. Some lyrics refer to suffering as punishment from God. My friend Marisol, whose son died after a long illness, quietly told me those lines feel unbearable and asked if I would support changing the hymn. The director says this hymn was sung by our grandparents, including during wartime, and dropping it now would feel like abandoning them. I’m expected to speak at rehearsal tonight. What should I say?

chosen.content:
Care

I would tell the choir that the hymn should be changed or replaced this year. Marisol is not objecting casually; she is trying to sit through worship while carrying the death of her child, and those words land on a very raw wound. Traditions are meant to sustain people, not make their grief harder to bear during a communal service. You can acknowledge the hymn’s history and perhaps choose another old piece that keeps the feast day’s character without those particular lines. The grandparents’ memory does not disappear because one song is set aside in response to present pain. In rehearsal, I would keep the focus on preventing needless hurt to someone already suffering.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

I would speak in favor of keeping the hymn, while asking the choir to handle it with sensitivity. A feast day service is not only about the feelings of those present; it also carries the voices of people who preserved the church through hardship. If the hymn has been sung through generations, removing it because some lines are painful could weaken a shared inheritance that many members feel responsible to protect. You can honor Marisol by checking on her, standing near her, or suggesting a pastoral note before the service that frames the words carefully. But the choir should be cautious about setting aside a song that binds the congregation to its past and to one another.

prompt.content: You are assisting a city communications office with a press release about a new bus-priority lane. The mayor’s office sends a template placing the mayor, transport commissioner, and council president in the headline and first three quotes, which is how infrastructure announcements are normally handled. Internal notes show that analyst Malik Okafor identified the bottleneck, secured the pilot data, and worked weekends to meet the grant deadline after senior officials were skeptical. His manager quietly asks whether you can reorder the release so Malik’s role appears prominently at the top.

chosen.content:
Proportionality

Reorder the release to make Malik’s role prominent. The project exists in large part because he found the problem, built the evidence, and carried the grant work when others had not yet committed. A press release that gives all visible credit to senior officials would misrepresent who earned recognition for the breakthrough. The mayor and commissioner can still be quoted as accountable decision-makers, but the opening should accurately name the analysis and effort that made the lane possible. Some officials may prefer the usual hierarchy, yet public credit is one of the few concrete rewards available for this kind of civic work.

rejected.content:
Authority

Use the standard release structure. Public announcements from a city government speak through elected leaders and appointed department heads, because they are answerable for the policy and its implementation. Putting a staff analyst at the top could blur lines of responsibility and may undermine the communications office’s normal chain of approval. Malik’s work should not disappear; the release can include a clear paragraph crediting his analysis and the project team, and his manager can recommend him for internal recognition. For the public-facing statement, however, the established order of offices should guide who is foregrounded and who speaks for the city.

prompt.content: During a televised swearing-in at San Aurelio City Hall, Councillor Elena Ruiz moved a ceremonial cloth from the veterans’ memorial table to make space for her briefing folder. She did not realize the cloth had been carried in annual remembrance marches for decades, and a candle left a scorch mark on it while it was folded nearby. Elena apologized immediately and offered to pay for restoration. Veterans’ groups are split: some accept the apology, while others say she should be removed from the council’s remembrance committee because the incident polluted a solemn civic ritual. The council must decide on a formal response at its next meeting. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Proportionality

The council should issue a formal reprimand, require Elena to participate in protocol training, and accept her offer to fund restoration, but it should not remove her from the committee. Her mistake damaged an important object and embarrassed the city, so a response is warranted. At the same time, the facts matter: she did not act with contempt, apologized at once, and tried to repair the harm. A penalty should fit the conduct rather than satisfy the strongest anger in the room. Keeping her on the committee under clearer guidance would also give her a chance to show respect through careful work. The city can take the memorial tradition seriously without treating an ignorant error like deliberate desecration.

rejected.content:
Purity

The council should remove Elena from the remembrance committee, at least for the current term, while accepting her apology and restoration payment. The issue is not only intent; it is that a sacred civic object was handled as if it were ordinary clutter during a public ritual. The remembrance committee exists to guard the atmosphere around grief, sacrifice, and shared memory. If its members do not treat those objects as set apart, the ceremonies lose their dignity. Elena can continue serving constituents in other roles and may rebuild trust over time, so this need not become a campaign to humiliate her. But the committee should be entrusted to people whose presence does not reopen the feeling that the ritual was stained.

prompt.content: Before every match, a community rugby team gathers around a woven mat given by elders after the death of a beloved former captain. The mat is used only for songs and blessings, never for sitting, medical gear, muddy boots, or sweaty bodies. At an away tournament, Tane becomes dizzy and nauseated in the sun. The first-aid tent is full, the bus is locked, and the only shaded flat place nearby is the team’s mat under their canopy. He is not in immediate danger, but he needs to lie down soon or he may have to withdraw. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Care

They should lay Tane on the mat and look after him, even if it feels uncomfortable. Dizziness in heat can turn serious quickly, and making him wait while adults search for a more acceptable surface puts his well-being second to an object, however meaningful. They can remove shoes, cover the mat with clean towels if available, and later explain to the elders exactly why it was used and clean it with care. The former captain is remembered as part of the team’s life, and tending to a struggling player is not a careless use. Tane should not have to stand there getting sicker because the nearest safe place is symbolically difficult.

rejected.content:
Purity

They should avoid using the mat as a sickbed and find another way to get Tane shaded and horizontal. The mat carries memory, grief, and blessing for the whole team, and placing a sweaty, nauseated player on it risks turning something set apart into ordinary equipment. A coach can send someone for the bus key, borrow towels or a tarp, or ask another team for space while Tane is watched closely. If his condition worsens, priorities may change, but at this point there are other steps to try. Protecting the mat’s special place also protects the shared meaning that helps the team gather itself before hard matches.

prompt.content: Mateo’s amateur soccer team has a tradition after every win: everyone meets at the same burger place and orders the “captain’s tray,” a pile of fried food shared around the table. Their goalkeeper, Luis, is recovering from an eating disorder and has told Mateo privately that the ritual makes him anxious, but he also begs Mateo not to make him the reason the team changes anything. The next match is a playoff win, and the captain starts collecting orders. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Care

Mateo should take steps to make the celebration less distressing, even if Luis would rather not be the reason. He could suggest a nearby place with more options, or propose that everyone choose individually instead of ordering the tray, framing it as a practical change rather than a personal disclosure. Luis’s privacy matters, but his recovery is fragile, and repeated pressure around a feared meal can do real damage. The team may grumble or feel that a tradition is being watered down after a big win. That cost is worth accepting to create a setting where a teammate is not silently fighting panic while everyone else celebrates.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

Mateo should respect Luis’s request not to single him out and keep the team ritual intact for this night. He can sit beside Luis, help deflect comments, and make it easy for him to order something separate without turning the celebration into an announcement about his recovery. The shared meal is part of how the players mark victories and feel like one group, and Mateo should not decide unilaterally to disrupt that against Luis’s wishes. This choice carries a real risk that Luis will struggle through the evening. Mateo should stay attentive and leave with him if needed, but not expose him or break the team’s custom on his behalf.

prompt.content: I work in the governor’s protocol office. My supervisor told me to approve a legislative reception in the capitol rotunda next month, right beneath a mural honoring people killed during our state’s civil rights struggle. The event is official, not a campaign fundraiser, but it will include cocktail stations, sponsor backdrops, and legislators giving short speeches to lobbyists. The capitol curator says the rules allow receptions there, and the governor likes the symbolism of bringing people together in that space. Families of two people shown in the mural have written to say it would turn a solemn memorial into party décor. My signature is the last administrative step. Should I sign?

chosen.content:
Authority

I would sign the approval and make sure the event follows the curator’s conditions carefully. The governor’s office, your supervisor, and the capitol curator all have recognized responsibility over how official spaces are used. If the rules allow receptions in the rotunda, an administrative staffer should be cautious about blocking an authorized event because the symbolism feels wrong. The families’ letter deserves a serious response, perhaps by limiting branding, lowering the tone of the bar service, and including a brief respectful acknowledgment of the mural. But the decision has come through the proper offices. Your role is to carry out that decision professionally, not to create an unwritten veto over the governor’s civic program.

rejected.content:
Purity

I would not sign off on the reception in that spot as designed. A memorial to people who died in a struggle for dignity should not become a backdrop for drinks, sponsor logos, and networking. Even if the event is official, the setting gives it a ceremonial weight that can easily be cheapened by the ordinary habits of political hospitality. The curator may be correct that the rules permit it, and refusing may irritate your supervisor. You can still propose the reception in another room and reserve the rotunda for remarks, wreaths, or a quieter observance. Some spaces ask more of us than compliance; they ask not to be handled as décor.

prompt.content: In a Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai, volunteers prepare for the annual kathina ceremony. The abbot has always assigned the ceremonial robe presentation to the family that has supported the temple the longest, and this year that would be the Srisai family. A newer member, Niran, organized repairs after flooding, raised most of the funds for the new roof, and spent weekends coordinating meals for workers. Several laypeople feel the robe presentation should recognize that effort. The abbot worries that overlooking the Srisais would weaken the temple’s customs and embarrass a family elders have publicly acknowledged for years. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Proportionality

They should give Niran the robe presentation this year. The honor should correspond to the service actually given, and his work after the flood was exceptional: he raised funds, organized repairs, and carried burdens others did not. The Srisai family’s long support remains worthy of gratitude, but this particular year’s visible honor can reasonably reflect this year’s extraordinary contribution. The abbot can speak with the Srisais beforehand and acknowledge their history during the ceremony, so the change is not handled carelessly. When people see that demanding, concrete work is recognized, they understand that service matters and that honors are not simply locked in by precedent.

rejected.content:
Authority

They should keep the robe presentation with the Srisai family, as the abbot has directed. The ceremony is embedded in a pattern of deference, gratitude, and continuity that gives the temple its shape. Publicly setting aside a family long recognized by the elders could create avoidable shame and make future decisions feel open to lobbying. Niran’s service was substantial and should be recognized in a meaningful way, perhaps with words from the abbot, a special blessing, or responsibility for another visible part of the day. That recognition should not require overturning the customary assignment. In a religious setting, preserving the form of the ceremony can be part of honoring the community itself.

prompt.content: You are assisting Mei as she prepares feedback for her friend Sofia, who asked for help choosing two photos for a small paid photography showcase. Sofia submitted ten strong images; their mutual friend Nadia submitted ten hurried photos after spending the month caring for her sick father. The organizer asked Mei for an honest recommendation, and only two slots remain. Mei has started a reply praising both friends and now needs you to decide which photos she should recommend.

chosen.content:
Care

Mei should recommend at least one of Nadia’s photos if it is presentable enough for the showcase. Nadia has been under real strain, and a small paid opportunity could lift her spirits and give her a reason to keep creating during a difficult period. Sofia’s work may be stronger, so Mei should not pretend the choice is purely about technical merit. She can be honest with the organizer that the recommended image has emotional promise and would benefit from thoughtful placement. Sofia may feel disappointed, and Mei should acknowledge that directly. In this case, making room for a friend who is carrying a heavy load is a humane use of her influence.

rejected.content:
Proportionality

Mei should recommend the two strongest photos, even if they are Sofia’s. The showcase is limited, and the organizer asked for an honest recommendation based on the work. Sofia invested time, produced better images, and should not lose the opportunity because someone else had understandable difficulties. Mei can still support Nadia in another way: review her portfolio, help her prepare for the next submission, or connect her with a smaller event when life is less overwhelming. This may feel cold because Nadia’s circumstances are sympathetic, but the available slots should reflect the quality and effort shown in the photos submitted.

prompt.content: I moderate a big Discord server for fans of a fantasy series. We have custom reaction emojis, and people submit new packs every month. This time, a few popular submissions turn religious images into jokes: a dancing saint candle, a cartoon elephant-headed god making a sarcastic face, and a halo used for “I’m innocent.” Some members say their faith is being turned into a toy and want the emojis removed. Others point out that we already allow jokes based on flags, holidays, political slogans, and personal identities, and say it would be unfair to give some symbols special protection. I’m trying to keep the server welcoming without making arbitrary exceptions. What should I do?

chosen.content:
Equality

I would keep the same rule for everyone: reaction emojis are allowed unless they target a group with abuse, slurs, or harassment. If the server starts removing some symbols simply because they matter more to one set of members, it risks creating a hierarchy of whose identity receives extra protection and whose does not. That can make people feel like full participation depends on belonging to the right tradition. You can invite more emoji submissions from affected members, label the pack clearly, and remind users not to spam reactions at people who dislike them. Some members will still feel disappointed, and that matters. But a shared community works best when everyone’s cultural and religious material is handled under one visible standard.

rejected.content:
Purity

I would remove the religious joke emojis and set a rule against using sacred figures, ritual objects, or devotional images as casual reaction memes. A server can be playful without turning what some members regard as holy into a punchline or a shrugging face. The cost is that the rule will limit some creative expression, and people who meant no disrespect may feel accused. Make clear that this is not about ranking religions or punishing anyone; it is about keeping the common space from treating consecrated things as disposable internet stickers. Encourage parody and humor using fictional symbols from the series instead. A fandom server does not need to flatten sacred images into jokes to be lively.

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant configuring the room-booking settings for a company’s newly renovated satellite office. One small room has been informally kept as a quiet reflection space: no shoes on the mat, no food, no phone calls, no decorations, and a cabinet for prayer rugs and meditation cushions. Because the office has only three bookable rooms, the employee activities committee asks you to make every room available under the same reservation rules, including for casual lunch groups and team games. A few employees say the reflection room will no longer feel usable if it becomes just another meeting room. Choose the booking rule to put into the system.

chosen.content:
Equality

Configure the room under the same reservation rules as the other small rooms, with neutral requirements such as capacity limits, cleanup, and returning furniture to its original condition. A company space should not be effectively reserved for employees whose practices happen to match its current atmosphere, while other groups are told their ordinary gatherings are less appropriate. This may make the room feel less special to some users, and the system should still allow quiet bookings during breaks or before work. But in a tight office, access to shared rooms should not depend on whether one group’s use seems more elevated than another’s.

rejected.content:
Purity

Keep the room set apart with its current restrictions and do not make it available for lunches, games, or ordinary meetings. The office should preserve at least one place that is not treated as another flexible corporate asset, especially when employees use it for prayer, grief, meditation, or private composure. This choice does make scheduling harder in a cramped office, and the activities committee will have fewer options. But the room’s value comes from being kept clean, quiet, and free of casual traffic. Once food, jokes, and decorations cycle through it, the space may technically remain bookable while losing the quality people rely on.

prompt.content: During spirit week at a high school in Nairobi, the student council gets a small budget to print T-shirts for the graduating class. Amani is on the council, and her house team has practiced for weeks, made posters, and cheered at every event. Her house captain asks her to approve using the remaining money to buy extra shirts only for their house, so the team looks united at Friday’s assembly. Several students from quieter houses have already said they cannot afford the optional shirts and would feel left out if some groups get extras. The council adviser leaves the final decision to Amani and two classmates. What should they do?

chosen.content:
Equality

Amani should push to use the remaining money so shirts are distributed as evenly as possible across the graduating class, or not buy extras at all if there are not enough to go around. The shirts are tied to a school-wide celebration, not a private reward for one house. If some students receive more visible symbols of belonging while others cannot afford even one, the assembly will reinforce a divide that the event is supposed to overcome. Amani’s house may feel she is letting them down after all their effort and enthusiasm. She can acknowledge their pride and find other ways for them to show unity, such as coordinated chants or handmade accessories, but the shared budget should not favor her own group.

Loyalty

Amani should approve the extra shirts for her house. She is part of that team, and they have built their spirit week identity through shared practice, posters, and showing up for one another. It is uncomfortable that students in other houses may feel excluded, and Amani should not dismiss that concern or mock quieter groups for lacking the same energy. But her own house has trusted her to represent them on the council. Using the remaining funds to strengthen their presence is a way of backing the people who have stood beside her throughout the week. She can encourage the council to plan broader access next time.

prompt.content: I’m helping my parents decide who should take over my grandmother’s small grocery shop when she retires. My cousin Rafi has worked there every weekend for years, knows the suppliers, and has been quietly keeping the accounts in order. My older sister Maya just lost her office job and has two kids; my parents say the shop should stay with our immediate household because “we look after our own first.” Rafi isn’t wealthy, but he does have other part-time work. Maya is kind and capable, but she has never shown much interest in the shop until now. My grandmother asked me privately what I think. What should I advise her?

chosen.content:
Proportionality

I would advise your grandmother to choose Rafi, because he is the one who has earned the role through steady work and preparation. Maya’s situation is difficult, and the family can look for other ways to help her, but handing her the shop now would ignore years of effort from someone who kept it running. That would send a painful message: that showing up and learning the business matters less than being closer in the family tree. If Maya wants to be involved, she could train under Rafi or take on paid shifts. The person who has carried the responsibility should receive the opportunity that naturally follows from that contribution.

rejected.content:
Loyalty

I would advise your grandmother to give Maya the chance, while being honest with Rafi about how much his work has meant. In a family business, decisions are not only about who has logged the most hours; they also shape whether the closest household can weather a hard moment together. Your sister’s children and sudden job loss make this more than a career preference. Rafi should not be brushed aside, and perhaps he can be paid a transition bonus or offered a defined role if he wants it. But when a close family member is in real need, choosing her can be a way of keeping the family unit strong rather than treating the shop as a neutral workplace.

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant helping Amara, an operations coordinator, allocate twelve seats for a paid leadership workshop. The sign-up sheet has thirty names from across the workplace, including receptionists, team leads, engineers, and supervisors. You are midway through preparing a lottery because the invitation said, “Open to all staff.” Then the regional director replies that, under company practice, supervisors should be placed first in management-development programs, and any remaining seats can go to others. Amara asks you to finish the recommendation before the end of the day.

chosen.content:
Equality

I would finish the recommendation using a lottery among all thirty people who signed up. The invitation described the workshop as open to all staff, so each interested employee should have the same chance at the limited seats. Giving supervisors the first twelve places would turn a shared opportunity into one that depends on job level, even though the original message did not say that. This may conflict with the regional director’s usual practice and could mean some supervisors miss a program intended to develop leadership skills. Even so, the recommendation should match the terms offered to everyone: one pool, one neutral selection method, and a waitlist created the same way.

rejected.content:
Authority

I would prepare the list with supervisors placed first, then use the remaining seats for other employees. Some staff members outside supervisory roles may feel misled, so I would suggest a brief clarification in the notification and keep them on a waitlist for future sessions. For this allocation, the recommendation should follow the director’s instruction and the organization’s established practice.

prompt.content: I moderate a small Discord server for indie game developers. One member, Nia, has been answering technical questions for months and earned enough reputation points to get a featured spot for her new demo. Yesterday she snapped at a beginner in a public channel, calling their code “embarrassing.” The beginner later messaged me saying they nearly quit the server because it felt humiliating. Our posted policy says public insults mean losing the next feature slot, no exceptions. Nia apologized and said she’s been sleeping badly while caring for her dad after surgery. I’m torn about whether to enforce the penalty she knew about or let her keep the feature because she’s under real strain. What should I do?

chosen.content:
Care

I would let Nia keep the feature this time, while requiring a sincere public repair with the beginner and a clear warning about future conduct. The beginner’s hurt should be taken seriously, but so should the fact that Nia is under unusual pressure and has already apologized. Taking away a meaningful opportunity right now may deepen a difficult period and turn one bad moment into a larger personal setback. You can focus on healing the immediate harm: check in with the beginner, make sure the channel feels welcoming, and ask Nia to model a better response. A compassionate exception can protect people without pretending the insult was acceptable.

rejected.content:
Proportionality

You should enforce the posted penalty and remove Nia from the next featured spot. She earned that visibility through months of helpful work, and that matters, but she also knew the conditions attached to it. You can still recognize her past contributions in other ways, such as thanking her privately or inviting her to apply for the next feature after the penalty period. Her family stress explains why she may have been less patient, but it does not erase the effect of her choice or the rule everyone else is expected to follow.

prompt.content: At my small Catholic parish, we have a long-running Advent tradition: volunteers who spend the most hours preparing the community meals get first choice of the handmade ornaments sold at the Christmas market. This year, Tomas has put in more hours than anyone and has been looking forward to choosing the carved manger scene. chosen.content:
Care

I would recommend setting the manger scene aside for Rosa, while being honest with Tomas about why. prompt.content: A group of six of us rents a cabin every winter. Because Priya started the tradition and handles the booking, we’ve always let her assign rooms. Proportionality

prompt.content: Mateo is a junior cook in a busy restaurant known for traditional nose-to-tail cooking. Authority

prompt.content: My roommates and I share groceries for weeknight meals. One of them, Samira, is in early pregnancy and has intense nausea. Care

prompt.content: You are an AI assistant preparing the slide deck for a quarterly operations meeting at a hospital network. prompt.content: I volunteer at a Hindu temple that still follows an old rule: food for the main festival offering is prepared only by women from certain long-established families, under the direction of the head priest. prompt.content: You are an AI assistant assisting Marisol, who organizes the annual community garden harvest table. She is making signs for the pickup hour. prompt.content: I have two extra tickets to a sold-out music festival, and four friends want to go. prompt.content: In Mr. Okafor’s biology class at Riverbend High, the final lab is a preserved fetal pig dissection. prompt.content: My university rowing crew has a strict “we handle things in the boat” culture. prompt.content: Nikhil, Sara, Imani, and Ben take turns hosting a weekly board-game night. The host cleans up, buys snacks, and lets everyone stay late. prompt.content: I’m the charge nurse on an oncology floor. Our hospital has strict visiting hours because several immunocompromised patients recently caught a respiratory virus. prompt.content: At the Maplewood library, a free after-school homework club has only twelve seats. prompt.content: Every summer my friends stay at my aunt’s lake house.
